newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to decide on food aid to N.Korea soon.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to decide on food aid to N.Korea soon.

text.p: South Korea on Wednesday was still undecided on the size of an aid package for hunger-stricken North Korea, government officials said just hours before a make-or-break meeting with the North.

"The government will make a further contribution to help relieve food shortages in North Korea. But we have yet to decide on the size of the additional donation," said Kwon Tae-myon, a director at the foreign ministry.
Seoul has said it does not want the world's last Stalinist dictatorship to implode, spilling out refugees and possibly igniting a war.

But on a visit to South Korea last week, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen agreed with Seoul leaders that they should not feed a nation that, while begging for food, pours scarce resources into a strong military and threatens South Korea with chemical-tipped missiles.

South Korea contributed $6 million and the United States $10 million to a World Food Programme (WFP) appeal for $41.6 million. On Tuesday, Washington announced it would give an extra $15 million after the WFP appeal was raised to $95.5 million.
"An announcement will be made in the near future on further food aid (from South Korea)," said spokesman Kang Ho-yang at Seoul's National Unification Ministry.
Pyongyang, swallowing its self-reliance ideology of "juche" to openly request international food aid, told U.N. officials this month that 134 children had died of malnutrition.

In a crucial meeting later on Wednesday in New York, North Korea is due to respond to South Korea and the United States, which jointly proposed four-nation peace talks exactly a year ago. The fourth participant is China.
The talks are aimed at securing a peace treaty to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

South Korean officials have said Pyongyang is expected to respond favourably but likely to seek concessions, particularly from the United States. North Korea wants diplomatic recognition from Washington and an easing of the U.S.trade embargo.
"A serious food shortage and economic difficulties will eventually push North Korea to the peace table," South Korean Deputy National Unification Minister Lee Ho told Reuters.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns denied the increase in food aid was politically motivated, saying even if Pyongyang did not agree to join the talks, the aid would go forward.
WFP assessments "have convinced us the food situation in North Korea will reach a critical stage this spring" with groups such as young children particularly at risk, he said.
Seoul officials say Pyongyang has previously demanded major food aid in return for an agreement to join peace talks.
A Pyongyang foreign ministry official on Saturday warned Washington and Seoul against using food aid as leverage.

The state Korean Central News Agency quoted the official as condemning what he described as "strange assertions" by Washington and Seoul that he felt stated food aid to the North could only be discussed once peace talks were opened.
"Raising such a condition is a dishonest and inhumanitarian behaviour aimed at abusing food aid as a political weapon and securing a concession from the DPRK in the security issue."
A Seoul official said: "Ironically, that statement opens the way for North Korea to drop its earlier demands for guarantees of substantial food aid in return for entering into the talks."
